Mechanic Called To Revive Old Mustang Parked in Garage 14 Years Ago, It's a 1968 Shelby GT500
51 photos
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled
“It all starts with a phone call about an old Mustang that needs some help getting back on the road.” Don’t they all? And, with millions of old Mustangs made in the moniker’s 62 years on assembly, it’s not even that exhilarating anymore. Except this old Mustang has had a few upgrades made to it before it was sold new. Some would argue it’s not even a Ford anymore, and they’d probably be right, because “S H E L B Y” is a funny way of spelling Ford, isn’t it?
Few childhood daydreams survive contact with adulthood, yet Brandon Cummings of the BeAircooled YouTube channel recently lived out the ultimate gearhead fantasy. As an 8-year-old boy gluing plastic valve covers onto a 1/25-scale Revell 428 model engine, and later as a 16-year-old teenager watching Steve McQueen pilot a Highland Green fastback in Bullitt, he never imagined wrenching on an identical 1968 Shelby GT500 inside his own Glenview, Illinois restoration shop.
The opportunity arrived through a casual phone call from a mutual buddy named Josh, who mentioned a friend named Chris looking to revive a dormant Mustang before putting it up for sale. Having wrenched on plenty of vintage Ford Broncos, trucks, and pony cars, Brandon agreed to help, only to learn that the sleeping machine was actually 1968 Shelby GT500 serial number 562, parked untouched in Chicago since late 2012.
Chris caught the collector car bug with a 1961 Ford Thunderbird convertible before seizing the chance to buy Shelby number #562 in the spring of 2001. Historical records revealed that this early-build 1968 fastback was originally ordered and delivered in late 1967 through JD Ball Ford in Miami, Florida. Over 25 years of dedicated ownership, Chris logged roughly 4,000 miles cruising strictly to local car shows around the Chicagoland area.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled During the first 12 or 13 years of his stewardship, Chris made the Highland Green muscle car a regular fixture at suburban gatherings. He hit Elmhurst on Wednesday evenings, Woodfire Chicken on Friday nights, Des Plaines on Saturdays, and Rand Red Hots whenever the weather cooperated. Once those weekly neighborhood cruise nights gradually dried up in 2012, he tucked the big-block pony inside his brick-and-timber city garage for 14 years.
Beyond driving the fastback locally, Chris spent the early 2000s traveling across America to attend Shelby conventions held at active racetracks, including Road America in Wisconsin, California Speedway in Rancho Cucamonga, Nashville, Raleigh-Durham in North Carolina, and the Volo Museum in Illinois. He met Carroll Shelby so frequently that the legendary Texan greeted him by first name, personally signing the dashboard above the passenger sea.
To preserve the car's originality, Chris fitted an aftermarket air cleaner lid over the Holley carburetor and carried the factory steel cover to the 30th Shelby American Automobile Club reunion in Riverside, California, in July 2005. There, both Carroll Shelby and Daytona Coupe racing driver Bob Bondurant autographed the original metal lid. Shelby also signed Chris's March 1957 Sports Illustrated issue celebrating his historic 24 Hours of Le Mans victory.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled The memorabilia archive accompanying number #562 even includes a hardbound book bearing 24 authentic signatures from key Shelby American pioneers. Alongside Carroll Shelby and Bob Bondurant, the pages feature autographs from project engineer Chuck Cantwell, team photographer Dave Friedman, surfboard shaper and fiberglass specialist Tweety, and Doyle Gammell, who worked as a teenager at Dean Moon's Speed Shop in 1962 installing the first Ford V8 into an aluminum AC Cobra.
Extracting the prized fastback from its long slumber proved urgent because Chris was preparing to demolish the aging wooden garage. With helpers bracing the fragile overhead door so it would not collapse onto the roof, Brandon guided the dusty green Mustang out into the Chicago daylight for the first time since 2012. A flatbed tow truck then hauled the time capsule to the BeAircooled shop for a thorough mechanical awakening.
Up on the shop lift, Brandon bypassed the temptation to crank the dry engine and started at the fuel tank beneath the undercoated chassis. After slicing the petrified outlet hose, he drained nearly 10 gallons of foul-smelling, yellow-tinted vintage gasoline that had soured over 14 years. Threading a borescope camera inside the tank revealed a spotless metal floor, clean upper baffles, and an intact sender float free of rust scale.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled Pulling all four cobweb-draped wheels exposed a braking system that demanded careful rejuvenation before taming a big-block Shelby on public streets. While the passenger-side rear drum was bone dry, a weeping differential axle seal had coated the driver-side backing plate and Ford-stamped shoes in sticky gear oil. Up front, green repaint overspray on the calipers and aging rubber lines prompted Brandon to send the entire hydraulic assembly to Phoenix Caliper.
While the front hydraulic disc brakes undergo restoration and the 428 V8 awaits an internal cylinder borescope inspection, number #562 stands as a proud monument to celebrated first-generation Shelby Mustang history. Spanning six model years from 1965 through 1970, the original lineage encompassed the small-block GT350, the track-bred GT350R, the Hertz GT350H rent-a-racer, the big-block GT500, the one-off 1967 Super Snake, and the mid-year 1968 GT500KR King of the Road.
Across that entire 1965 to 1970 first-generation run, total Shelby Mustang output reached 13,912 vehicles (including race, prototype, test mules, and preproduction examples). Annual production totaled 562 fastbacks in 1965, 2,378 cars in 1966, 3,225 units in 1967, and a peak of 4,451 vehicles in 1968, followed by 3,294 cars built for 1969, of which 789 unsold examples received updated 1970 vehicle identification numbers.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled Offered across four model years from 1967 through 1970, the GT500 line accounted for 7,184 units. That big-block tally comprises 2,048 fastbacks in 1967, 1,423 standard GT500s and 1,571 GT500KRs in 1968, and 2,541 GT500s across 1969 (1,872 copies) and 1970 (470 cars). Regular production body styles included two-door fastbacks, renamed SportsRoof in 1969, and two-door convertibles offered from 1968 to 1970, alongside two experimental notchback coupes.
Most of those were the iconic fastbacks (5,938), leaving 1,246 ragtops on the table. Irrespective of body style, all GT500s made in the classic era had a 428 cubic-inch big-block V8 underhood. The 1967 GT500 debuted with a 355-horsepower 428 “Police Interceptor” V8 and dual four-barrel carburetors.
The lone 1967 Super Snake packed a 427-cubic-inch V8 (it’s the sole exception to the 428 rule, although the 427 Side oiler was offered as an option on the GT500). Early 1968 GT500s used a single four-barrel 360-horsepower 428 Police Interceptor before the 335-horsepower 428 Cobra Jet and Super Cobra Jet powered 1968 GT500KRs and all the 1969/1970 models. Transmissions were available in 4-speed Toploader manual or 3-speed C6 automatic variants.
Photo: YouTube/BeAircooled Breaking down the 4,451 Shelbys built for 1968, Marti Auto Works records document 1,457 small-block GT350s, all powered by the 250-horsepower J-code 302-cubic-inch V8. That total splits into 1,053 fastbacks (including 224 automatic Hertz cars), with 445 manual 4-speeds and 608 C4 3-speed automatics, plus 404 convertibles comprising 214 manual 4-speeds and 190 C4 3-speed automatics.
Standard 1968 GT500 production with the S-code 428 Police Interceptor V8 reached 1,423 units: 1,020 fastbacks comprising 405 manual 4-speeds and 615 C6 3-speed automatics, and 402 convertibles with 153 manuals and 249 automatics. Finally, the R-code 428 Cobra Jet powered 1,571 GT500KRs, dividing 1,053 fastbacks into 530 manuals and 523 automatics, plus 518 convertibles with 267 manuals and 251 automatics.
Brandon, the YouTubing mechanic, will document the revival of #562 over several episodes, so stay tuned. As for Chris, the owner of the car, he’s getting ready to end 25 years of meticulous ownership. I’ll keep an eye out for this car, if it goes on public sale again. “Again,” as in it was sold at a Kruse auction in May of 1991, for $22,201. You tell me if that was a lot of money for a 1968 Shelby GT500 back then, but bear in mind that it’s Canadian dollars. At the exchange rate of the time, it was about $19,300 USD.
